tracks.label: Opening
tracks.text: Chapter 2. Flight. Somewhere over Africa, on a winter day in Europe, a Common Swift (Apus apus) is flying, and it has probably not touched the ground for months. Swedish researchers fitted swifts with data loggers weighing about a gram and recaptured the birds when they came back to breed. The loggers showed that the swifts had stayed airborne for about ten months of the year, landing for less than 1 percent of that time; some never landed at all. They fed on insects caught in the air, and the birds that never landed even grew new flight feathers on the wing. Staying up that long is possible only because of the physics of a wing, and because of the shape of the swift’s own wings: long, narrow and swept back like a crescent. That physics, and what wing shape reveals, is where this chapter begins. Chapter 1 showed you a body built for flight: feathers with locked vanes, fused bones, a keeled sternum and the large flight muscles it anchors. This chapter shows how that equipment flies. Section 2.1 explains the four forces on a flying bird and how a wing makes lift. Section 2.2 reads wing shape as a clue to a bird’s way of life, using two simple measurements, aspect ratio and wing loading. Section 2.3 compares flapping, gliding, soaring and hovering and what each one costs, with evidence from wind tunnels, tracking tags and heart-rate recorders. Section 2.4 asks why some birds gave flight up. The ideas return often: in Chapter 3 on the energy that flight burns, in Chapter 4 where flight style and silhouette become field marks, and in Chapter 7 on migration.

tracks.label: 2.1 Lift, drag and the wing
tracks.text: Section 2 point 1. Lift, drag and the wing. Four forces act on a bird in flight. Weight pulls it straight down. Lift, made by the wings, acts at right angles to the oncoming air. Drag, the resistance of the air, acts backward along the direction of motion. Thrust, the forward push that balances drag, comes from flapping. A gliding bird has no thrust at all. It trades height for distance, sloping gently downward so that lift tilts slightly forward and helps pull it along against drag, as Figure 2.1 shows. When the four forces balance, the bird flies at a steady speed; when they do not, it speeds up, slows down, climbs or sinks. Cut through a bird’s wing from front to back and you see an airfoil: rounded at the leading edge, thin at the trailing edge, and usually cambered, curved so that the upper surface bulges more than the lower. The wing meets the air at a slight tilt called the angle of attack. As air flows past, the curved, tilted wing bends the flow. Air can follow a curved path only if pressure pushes it around the curve, so the pressure above the wing falls below that of the surrounding air and the pressure below rises a little. That pressure difference, acting over the whole wing, is lift. The same flow can be described another way: the wing throws a large mass of air downward, the downwash, and by Newton’s third law the air pushes the wing up. These are two accounts of one event, not rival theories. Engineers sum up what lift depends on in one equation: lift = ½ times air density times airspeed² times wing area times lift coefficient. Air at sea level has a density of about 1.225 kilograms per cubic meter, so a cubic meter of air has a little more mass than a liter of water. The lift coefficient captures the wing’s shape and angle of attack. The squared speed matters most. Double the airspeed with everything else unchanged and lift rises fourfold; halve it and lift falls to a quarter. That is why an American Robin (Turdus migratorius) taking off from a lawn beats its wings so hard: at low speed it has little airflow to work with. It also explains why thin air at high altitude makes flight harder, a problem you will meet in Chapter 3. Tilting the wing more steeply raises the lift coefficient, but only up to a point. Beyond it the air can no longer follow the curved upper surface; it breaks away in swirls, lift collapses and drag soars. This is a stall. Birds come close to stalling every time they land, flying slowly with their wings steeply tilted, and they carry a device that helps. The alula is a small tuft of stiff feathers on the bird’s thumb, at the front of the wing near the wrist; watch a pigeon coming in to land and you may see it spring out from the leading edge. In 2015 a team in Seoul tested magpie wings in a wind tunnel with and without the alula raised. Raising it increased lift and often delayed the stall, because it set up a small swirl of air that kept the flow attached to the upper surface. Drag comes in two main kinds. Profile drag, together with drag on the body, comes from air rubbing past the bird and being pushed aside; it grows with the square of speed, which is why fast fliers are smooth and streamlined. Induced drag is the price of making lift. Because pressure is higher below the wing than above it, air spills around each wingtip and rolls up into a trailing wingtip vortex. Induced drag is largest at low speed, when the wing must work hardest, and it is smaller for long wings, which spread the work over a wider sweep of air. Much of what we know about these forces in birds comes from wind tunnels. In the 1960s Colin Pennycuick trained pigeons to glide in a tilting wind tunnel so that he could measure their gliding at different speeds, the start of a long effort to turn bird flight into a measurable science. A common misconception: The air going over the top of the wing has farther to travel, so it has to speed up to meet the air from underneath at the back edge. In fact, Nothing forces the two streams to meet again. Smoke tests in wind tunnels show the air over the top reaching the trailing edge well before the air underneath. Lift comes from the wing bending the airflow: curved flow needs lower pressure above the wing, and the air leaves the wing turned downward.

tracks.label: 2.2 Wing shapes and what they tell you
tracks.text: Section 2 point 2. Wing shapes and what they tell you. Lay the wing of a grouse beside the wing of a swift and the difference is obvious: one is short and broad, the other long and narrow. Wing shape is a record of how a bird lives. In 1957 the naturalist D. B. O. Savile sorted bird wings into four broad types, and his scheme is still the usual starting point (Figure 2.2). Two measurements make the comparison exact. Aspect ratio is wingspan squared divided by wing area; for a rectangle it is simply length divided by width, so long, narrow wings score high. Wing loading is the bird’s weight divided by its wing area. From the lift equation in section 2.1, a bird with high wing loading must fly faster to stay up, while a high aspect ratio cuts induced drag and makes gliding efficient. Elliptical wings are short and broad, with rounded tips and a low aspect ratio. They belong to gamebirds such as grouse and to most songbirds that live among trees and shrubs. They give a fast, steep takeoff and tight turns in cluttered places, at the cost of efficiency over long distances; a grouse bursting from the forest floor is the classic case. High-speed wings are pointed, often swept back, and taper to the tip. Falcons, swifts, swallows and shorebirds have them, and they suit fast, efficient flapping flight. The extreme case is the Common Swift. Its loggers, described at the start of this chapter, showed it airborne for about ten months of the year, landing for less than 1 percent of that time. High-aspect-ratio wings are long, narrow and pointed, the wings of seabirds that glide for hours over open ocean, such as albatrosses and shearwaters. They have very low induced drag and glide superbly, but they are poor for taking off and turning in tight spaces. The Wandering Albatross (Diomedea exulans) has the longest wingspan of any living bird, around 3 meters. Albatrosses travel by dynamic soaring, drawing energy from the wind itself. In 2012 researchers tracked free-flying Wandering Albatrosses with high-precision GPS and showed how: each bird repeats an up-and-down swooping curve, adjusted to the wind, that gains energy from the difference in wind speed near the waves and higher up. Slotted high-lift wings are broad, with large area, and their outer primary feathers spread apart at the tip like fingers, leaving gaps called slots. Eagles, hawks, vultures and condors have them. Their low wing loading lets them fly slowly and circle tightly inside rising air, and the slotted tips are thought to reduce induced drag and help keep the airflow attached at low speed. Broad wings also give the lift needed to take off from the ground, sometimes carrying prey. Look up at a soaring hawk or vulture and count the separated primaries at each wingtip; the slots are easy to see against the sky. These types are more than a convenient filing system. In 2020 Catherine Sheard and colleagues measured the hand-wing index, a measure of how long and pointed a wing is, for 10,338 species, more than 99 percent of living birds. Pointed wings were commoner in migratory birds and at high latitudes, where seasons are strongly marked, and rounder wings in territorial birds that stay put. Wing shape is therefore a clue you can use in the field. A long, pointed wing hints at a long-distance traveler or an aerial hunter; a short, rounded one at a bird of dense cover. Chapter 4 uses these silhouettes for identification, and Chapter 7 returns to the wings of migrants. A common misconception: Pointed wings are good wings; birds with short, rounded wings are just weak fliers. In fact, Every wing shape is a trade-off. Short, rounded wings give the explosive takeoff and tight turns a grouse or a sparrow needs among branches, which a long-winged albatross cannot match. No single shape is best at everything.

tracks.label: 2.3 Flapping, gliding, soaring and hovering
tracks.text: Section 2 point 3. Flapping, gliding, soaring and hovering. In flapping flight the wing does two jobs at once: it supports the bird and pushes it forward. On the downstroke, powered by the pectoralis muscle you met in Chapter 1, the wing sweeps down and forward, and because it moves through the air at an angle, the force on it tilts forward, giving both lift and thrust. On the upstroke, driven by the supracoracoideus, most birds bend the wing at the wrist and draw it in toward the body to cut drag. In slow flight most birds get essentially all of their weight support from the downstroke. Many small birds, such as finches and woodpeckers, alternate bursts of flapping with brief pauses on folded wings, which gives their flight its bounding, undulating look. Aerodynamic theory predicts that the power needed for flapping flight follows a U-shaped power curve (Figure 2.3). At low speed, induced power is high, because the wings must throw a great deal of air downward to stay up. At high speed, the power needed to overcome profile and body drag rises steeply. In between lies a minimum-power speed, the cheapest way to stay aloft, and a somewhat faster maximum-range speed, the best way to cover distance on a fixed amount of fuel. Testing this on live birds is hard. In 2003 Bret Tobalske and colleagues flew cockatiels and ringed turtle-doves in a wind tunnel with sensors that recorded the force and length change of the pectoralis muscle. The cockatiel’s curve was strongly U-shaped, the dove’s shallower, and an earlier study of magpies had found a nearly flat curve over most speeds. Theory gets the general shape right, but each species’ wings and wingbeat bend the curve. A gliding bird holds its wings out and does not flap. Without thrust it must lose height, and its glide ratio, the distance it travels forward for each meter it sinks, equals its ratio of lift to drag. Soaring is gliding in air that rises at least as fast as the bird sinks. Over land, soaring birds circle in thermals, columns of warm air rising from sunlit ground, or ride updrafts where wind meets a ridge; over the ocean, albatrosses use dynamic soaring (section 2.2). Soaring is remarkably cheap. In 2020 Hannah Williams and colleagues fitted eight young Andean Condors (Vultur gryphus) with recorders that logged every wingbeat. Across more than 216 hours of flight the condors flapped for only about 1 percent of the time, mostly during takeoff, and one bird flew for five hours, covering about 172 kilometers, without flapping. Heart-rate recorders tell the same story at sea. Wandering Albatrosses flying with the wind behind them or from the side had heart rates, a measure of energy use, close to those of birds resting on land; flying into a headwind, taking off and landing cost far more. Where there is no rising air and no strong wind to exploit, a bird must flap. Bar-tailed Godwits (Limosa lapponica) leaving Alaska in autumn cross the Pacific toward New Zealand and eastern Australia without stopping. Satellite tags on seven females recorded nonstop flights of 8,117 to 11,680 kilometers lasting six to nine days, along a route the researchers described as a wind-assisted corridor. Chapter 7 follows these flights in detail. Hovering, holding still in the air, is the most expensive mode of all, because the bird has no forward speed and its wings must create all the airflow themselves (the left end of Figure 2.3). Hummingbirds are the specialists. A hovering hummingbird holds its body steeply upright and sweeps its wings forward and back, turning each wing over at the end of the stroke so that the backstroke makes lift too. In 2005 Douglas Warrick and colleagues used a laser to light up tiny particles in the air around hovering Rufous Hummingbirds (Selasphorus rufus) and filmed the swirling wake. About 75 percent of the weight support came from the downstroke and 25 percent from the upstroke, unlike insects, which split it about evenly, and unlike other birds, which rely on the downstroke alone when flying slowly. A Ruby-throated Hummingbird (Archilochus colubris) beats its wings more than 50 times a second as it hovers at a flower; the fuel this burns is a subject of Chapter 3. A common misconception: Gliding and soaring are the same thing. In fact, A gliding bird always sinks relative to the air around it. Soaring is gliding in air that rises at least as fast as the bird sinks, as in a thermal or a ridge updraft, or drawing energy from wind, as albatrosses do. A gliding bird must eventually land or flap; a soaring bird can stay up for hours.

tracks.label: 2.4 Flightless birds
tracks.text: Section 2 point 4. Flightless birds. Flight is enormously useful, and it is also expensive to keep. Flight muscles are large and costly to maintain, and a flying body limits how heavy a bird can become. Where flight stops paying for itself, birds lose it. Living flightless birds include the ratites (ostriches, rheas, the Emu, cassowaries and kiwis), the penguins, and a scattering of island species such as the Kakapo, a heavy, ground-dwelling parrot of New Zealand, and a number of rails. Each case is a natural experiment: it shows which parts of the flying body disappear when they are no longer needed, and which stay. The ratites show what happens when flight goes. As Chapter 1 showed, they have a flat sternum without a keel and small flight muscles. Their wings are reduced, in kiwis to stubs hidden in the plumage, and their feathers lack the hooked barbules that lock a vane into one surface, so ostrich plumes are soft and loose. Ratites were long thought to share a single flightless ancestor that rode the pieces of the southern supercontinent Gondwana as it broke apart. DNA has overturned that idea. The tinamous of Central and South America, which can fly, sit inside the ratite family tree. In 2014 a team that recovered DNA from bones of the extinct elephant birds of Madagascar found that their closest relatives were the kiwis of New Zealand, not the ostriches of nearby Africa. The simplest explanation is that ratite ancestors could fly, spread across oceans, and lost flight several times over. Islands are where flight is lost most often. Where there are no rats, cats or other ground predators, a bird that walks risks little, and a bird that stops building big flight muscles saves energy. In 1994 Brian McNab showed that flightless island rails have unusually low resting metabolic rates, and that the rates fall as their flight muscles shrink; kiwis show the same pattern. The smallest flightless bird alive, the Inaccessible Island Rail (Atlantisia rogersi), weighs about 40 grams, less than a chicken’s egg, and lives only on Inaccessible Island in the South Atlantic. Its DNA shows that its closest relatives are small rails of South America that can fly, and that its ancestor reached the island about 1.5 million years ago. It must have flown there, then lost the ability. Flight can be lost quickly. The Galápagos Cormorant (Phalacrocorax harrisi, now often placed in the genus Nannopterum) is the only flightless species among about 40 cormorants, and it split from flying relatives within the last 2 million years. When Alejandro Burga and colleagues compared its genome with those of flying cormorants in 2017, they found changes in genes needed for the primary cilium, a tiny structure on cells that helps control skeletal growth. In people, faults in such genes cause skeletal disorders, often with unusually short limbs. A small number of genetic changes, in other words, can shrink a wing. Penguins took a different path. They gave up flight in air but kept a deep keel and powerful flight muscles, because they use their wings to fly underwater. McNab found that, unlike flightless rails, penguins do not have low metabolic rates, which fits their continued use of the wings for locomotion. Loss of flight has a darker side, too. Many island flightless birds, from the Dodo of Mauritius, a giant relative of pigeons, to the moa of New Zealand, vanished after people arrived, through hunting and the predators people brought. Chapter 8 returns to that story. A common misconception: Flightless birds are primitive birds whose ancestors never learned to fly. In fact, Every flightless bird alive descends from flying ancestors. Feathers came before flight (Chapter 1), flight came next, and flightlessness evolved later, many separate times, in ratites, penguins, rails, a parrot, a cormorant and others.
